papers.title: Aging and Structural Change: Cost Disease in the Care Sector
papers.abstract: For most of the service sector, market productivity growth has pulled production out of the home. We show that formal nursing care is an exception because its productivity growth has been negative. A two-sector general equilibrium overlapping generations model with informal care attributes the rise in formal care's relative price to this decline, not demography. Care/non-care complementarity dominates formal/informal complementarity. As formal prices rise, elders substitute non-care consumption for formal care, shifting care onto informal caregivers. Population aging need not slow growth if non-care productivity rises or entering cohorts grow and its effects are offset by declining care needs.

papers.title: Clouds of Credit: Mapping the Financial Web Behind AI Compute
papers.abstract: We map the financial network supporting the AI buildout. Substantial equity cushions protect creditors against large obligations outstanding in mid-2026, but concentrated exposures and interconnected claims create weak links. Our calibrated model supports a large compute expansion in the coming years. The equilibrium investment exceeds the social optimum because firms do not internalize their effects on competitors' revenues. Debt finances nearly 60% of the expansion, increasing leverage, while non-recourse borrowing leaves project lenders exposed despite equity buffers. In the low-productivity state, losses reach $16.8 trillion across shareholders and creditors, with 40% loss-given-default on debt. Suppressing contractual payment spillovers among the key firms reduces private losses by approximately 30%, revealing substantial network propagation.

papers.title: Will AI Growth Reach the Developing World?
papers.abstract: This paper explores how economic growth driven by AI will impact the developing world. Our analysis is based on a growth model of a developed and developing economy where AI services are traded on the world market, and may substitute for or complement different labor inputs in production. Preferences allow for the possibility that demand for services provided by AI has an upper bound. The model predicts that developing countries may not benefit as much from AI-driven growth. First, they may lack complementary skills needed to fully utilize AI domestically. Second, they may be priced out of world markets due to their relatively lower productivity. We use our model to simulate how growth and welfare are affected by making workers more complementary to AI, subsidizing compute, speeding technology diffusion, and providing cash transfers. Numerical simulations of the model suggest that the potential for developing countries to be left behind – or having some workers lose in absolute terms – is substantial enough that researchers should study the impacts of AI on developing countries in real time.

papers.title: Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy
papers.abstract: We use the Phelps-Winter customer market—providing a better theory of price determination for large parts of the economy than the standard model—to show that raising interest rates induces higher prices, as firms value current profits more, and are more willing to lose customers for short-term gains. These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation. The weakening effectiveness of monetary policy was predicted by our earlier work on banks and the supply of credit, as a result of the elimination of interest prohibition on deposits; and further suggested by work on the structural transformation of the economy, as customer markets become more important.

papers.title: An Odd Approximation of Inflation for State Dependent Pricing Models
papers.abstract: We derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models with random menu costs and strategic complementarities. The representation, derived from first principles, replaces the cross-sectional distribution of price gaps with a finite set of its moments (the first three), while preserving the key economic forces of state-dependent pricing--movements in the frequency of price adjustment and selection. Along the impulse response, inflation is an odd (cubic) polynomial in the average price gap. Embedded in a general equilibrium setting, the model can be solved by perturbation, filtered, and estimated with standard DSGE tools, and it matches well the global solution across shock sizes. Applied to the 2021--22 inflation surge in the United States and the euro area, it shows that much of the variation that linear models would attribute to cost-push shocks is in fact endogenous amplification through the frequency of price changes and selection.
